card lp-overseer  [decided]
An overseer keeps an agent from getting stuck
why: A second process reads the event log in real time.
subtree: 12 cards, 12 decided

The goal: no agent stays stuck, whatever the cause. The overseer watches every running agent session and acts on three signs:

1. A permission prompt that nobody answers. The agent waits and does nothing else.
2. An unintentional loop. The agent repeats the same tool call, or the same failing check, and makes no progress.
3. A tool call with no timeout. A command that never returns holds the session forever.

It is the real safety control for auto-merge.

card vi-board-session-file  [decided]
A builder session runs only while the board log says it started and its process is still alive
why: A builder runs in its own process and can die without a word, for example when a person kills it by hand. A flag in a log alone then says it still runs, and the ticket pulses forever. So the board also checks the process itself, and keeps the agent's many lines out of the board log so that log stays a short record of ticket state.

The pulse and the live preview (#vi-board) mean that a builder session runs right now. The board needs a test for "runs now" that a dead process cannot fool.

**When a session runs.** The board log records when a session starts and when it ends (#vi-board-state). The start names the builder process. A session counts as running only while both hold:

- the board log has a start for it and no end yet;
- the named process is still alive.

When a builder process exits without writing its end, the server writes the end for it (#vi-board-details). A process that dies with no one to see it — killed from a terminal, or started before a server restart — fails the second test, so its ticket stops pulsing at once.

**Where the agent's lines go.** Each session writes the agent's stream to its own session log, one line

card lp-stateless  [decided]
The loop is stateless per pass
why: Long contexts degrade. The file system and git do not.

One fresh agent per pass. Give it the brief, the decision, the rubric, and the last failure. It does one unit of work and exits. The repository is the memory.

This changes the engine's shape: no agent lives longer than one pass.

**How a pass works:**

1. The loop makes one worktree from a snapshot of the working tree.
2. Pass n starts a fresh `claude -p` in the worktree. The prompt holds the brief, the decided cards in its depends_on closure, and the last failure: the failed command and the end of its output, cut to about 4,000 characters.

card vi-board-details  [decided]
Board details: where archive lives, the run strip, and the live preview
why: Small readings the board cards leave open, recorded so a later change can see them.

- Archive is a button in the drawer header, not on the board card. For a building ticket it is the only way to end the build (#werk-board-control).
- The live preview shows one summarised line per stream event, overseer lines included, not raw JSON.
- When a build child exits while its ticket is still live, the server ends the build: error for an exit code, stopped for a signal.
- A line above the columns shows G2 per run, waiting or passed, with the command that passes it. The board has no approve button, because the board does no editing.
- Importing ticket files makes ids the way planning does, <run>/<NN>, and adds nothing on a second run.
- While the drawer is open, each column shrinks to its cards and shows two at most; the rest scroll inside the column, so the drawer sits close under the board.
- The drawer header has two lines: the id, the running dot and the controls first, the title under them. A building ticket's time in the column shows only in the bar above the log, not in the header.
- The sidebar has a toggle in its top right corner that folds it to a narrow rail. The log has a toggle in its top right corner that hides the sidebar and doubles the log height. Both choices stay across redraws and page loads.
- Each log line shows its full time, top-aligned, in a column wide enough for it.

card st-build-run  [decided]
The merge loop: queue one ticket, merge it on green checks, then run the held-out set
why: Each ticket is green alone. Only a check on the run's tree plus the ticket shows whether they are green together.
subtree: 12 cards, 1 open, 11 decided

The coordinator takes the finished tickets one at a time, through a merge queue. #st-build-run-mechanics gives how the merge loop does it.

1. Make a temporary tree: the run's tree plus the ticket.
2. Run the checks on the temporary tree. Red: nothing merges, and the ticket goes back to the builder loop with the failure.
3. Green: the ticket merges.
4. Run the held-out set on the run's tree. This step belongs to validate, not build (#st-validate-heldout). A red step files a follow-up ticket, and the merge stands.

Build ends when every ticket is merged and every held-out step passes (#st-g2-heldout).

  -> refines         st-build-steps  Build: a builder loop per ticket and a merge loop per run

But the build process itself can die: a kill, a crash, a machine sleep. Nothing inside that process can see its own death, so the server, which already checks whether each build process is alive, writes the end and starts a fresh pass from the work already committed on the ticket's branch." --parent st-build-steps --status open --who you --body "**The problem.** A ticket whose build process died sits in building with no pulse (#vi-board-session-file). Nobody starts it again, so the run stops until a person sees it.

**The answer.** The server is the watcher. It looks for a dead build at two moments: when a build process it started exits, and when the server itself starts. A build counts as dead when the board log has a start for it, no end, and its process is gone. For each one the server does three things. It writes the end, with died as the reason. It starts a fresh pass of the same ticket, from the last commit on the ticket's branch, with the death as the last failure in the brief (#lp-stateless). The fresh pass counts against the ticket's retry cap, so a build that dies on every pass still stops (#st-build-silence-act treats a silent pass the same way).

A pass does not resume the agent's own conversation. Work the dead pass did not commit is lost: at most one pass of work. The session id stays in the session log for a person who wants to read what the dead pass did.

While the server is down, nothing watches. A build keeps running without the server; a build that dies in that time is found when the server starts again.

**Example.**

- Ticket T \"r/03\" sits in building. Its branch has two commits from earlier passes.
- Pass 3 runs in process P. It has edited files and not committed them.

1. A person closes the laptop lid. P dies. The server is down too.
2. The person starts werk. The server reads the board log: pass 3 of T started, has no end, and P is dead.
3. The server writes the end of pass 3: died. The edits that pass 3 did not commit are gone.
4. The server starts pass 4 of T from the second commit. The brief says that pass 3 died.
5. Pass 4 is the last pass the retry cap allows. If it dies too, T stops with died as the reason, and the server starts nothing more.
6. A build whose process is alive is left alone, whether this server started it or an earlier one did.

\`\`\`
board log for T            process     server action
-----------------          -------     -------------------------------------
pass 3 started (P)         P alive     none                          (before step 1)
no end                     P dead      (server is down)              (step 1)
no end                     P dead      write end: died               (steps 2-3)
pass 4 started (P2)        P2 alive    started from commit 2         (step 4)

dead = started, no end, process gone
fresh pass = new agent, last commit of the branch, death in the brief, counts against the cap
\`\`\`"

I proposed one card for this: **#st-build-died**. It is a ghost and status open, and it waits for your ✓.

The code already handles part of this:

1. **werk dies mid-build: no harm.** The server starts each build and the merge loop as separate processes. They keep running without the server and write their own events to the board log. After a restart, the server finds them again by the process id in the board log.
2. **The overseer cannot be the watcher.** It is a timer inside the build process (#lp-overseer-mechanics). When that process dies, the overseer dies with it.
3. **The build process dies: nothing restarts it.** The ticket stops pulsing, but it stays in building. The run stops until a person sees it.

The proposed card closes item 3. The server becomes the watcher. It looks for dead builds when a build process exits and when the server starts. For each dead build, it writes the end ("died") and starts a fresh pass from the last commit on the ticket's branch. That pass counts against the retry cap.

I recommend against keeping the Claude session id to resume the conversation (`:opt1`). A pass is stateless (#lp-stateless): the branch holds the work. A resume brings back a long context and a half-done step. The most it saves is one pass of uncommitted work. The session id stays in the session log, so a person can still read what the dead pass did.

Two other options are on the card:
- `:opt0`: the overseer restarts the build. It cannot, because it dies with the build process.
- `:opt2`: a person restarts the build by hand. The cost is that a death at night stops the run until morning.

All four cards that #st-build-died depends on are decided and not stale.

Next: open #st-build-died. Accept it, or tell me if you prefer `:opt2`, the restart by hand.

/**
 * `werk build <ticket-id>`: the builder loop for one ticket. See #st-build-ticket.
 *
 * One ticket, one worktree, fresh passes (#lp-stateless):
 *
 *   1. Implement. A fresh builder agent gets the brief and the last failure, nothing else.
 *   2. Check. The ticket's checks run, one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
 *   3. The gates: the grader (#lp-prod-judge), then the quality review (#lp-prod-review).
 *
 * A fail at any step starts a new pass at step 1, with the failure in its brief. The retry cap
 * stops the loop. A session that goes silent is cancelled by the overseer and the next pass is
 * told why (#st-build-silence-act); it counts against the cap.
 *
 * Before any code, the command appends a card obligation to the project's log (#st-build-card).
 * The ticket's state goes to the board (src/board.ts): started, one event per pass, ended, and
 * a move to merging on green. The merge itself belongs to the merge loop (#st-build-run).
 *
 * The base is the tip of the main line, the branch `main`, never a snapshot of a working tree:
 * tickets build from and merge onto the main line, with no integration branch of their own
 * (#st-plan-main, #werk-base-branch). Without that branch the build refuses. The ticket's own
 * branch `werk-build/<loop run>` is kept after the run; its worktree is not.
 *
 * The main line, the worktree and the branch belong to the target repository; the ticket
 * text, the board and the logs to the map's (#st-build-target).
 */

I decided #st-build-died and changed the code to match it. When a build process dies, the server now ends that build as `died` and starts the run again from the work the build had already committed. The type check passes, and all 783 tests pass.

How it works:
1. **Finding a dead build.** The server checks at two moments: when a build process it started exits, and when the server starts. A build counts as dead when its session has a start, no end, and no live process. A build under `werk run` does not record a process of its own, so the server checks the run's process.
2. **Restarting.** The server writes the end as `died` and starts `werk run` again, once per run. It does not start a second run while one is still alive. The merge loop builds the tickets in building first.
3. **The fresh pass.** It starts from the ticket's branch, which has every pass the dead build committed. Its brief says that the last pass died. Changes that the dead pass did not commit are gone.
4. **The retry cap.** The dead pass counts against the cap. When the cap is used up, the merge loop takes the ticket out of the build, the same as any other ticket at its cap.

I recorded a kill criterion for the card, because the card could not become decided without one. If a restarted build dies again on most of its passes, the decision changes to `:opt2`, a person restarts the build by hand.

One limit remains: a build that dies is found only at the two moments in item 1. If you started the build from a terminal and it dies while the server is up, the server finds it only at its next start.
